transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-04-06 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood Solutions Eng), Aisha Rahman (CTO, ForgeWorks), Benji Ortiz (Platform Lead), Claire Ng (SRE), Tommy Park (ML Eng)

Summary:
ForgeWorks is evaluating an onramp path to Redwood for their inference layer. Primary questions: hosted vs dedicated economics, private/VPC constraints, SDK compatibility with their LangChain/LlamaIndex based stack, gateway/proxy placement, rate limits and tenant quotas, and what observability hooks Redwood exposes for tracing and token-level cost visibility. They have regulatory requirements (SOC2 + data residency in EU) and prefer VPC-first architectures.

Topics covered:
- High level Redwood product modes (hosted / dedicated / private) and tradeoffs
- SDK language support, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, sidecar vs gateway approaches
- Rate limiting, tenant quotas, burst capacity and backpressure behaviors
- Observability: token-level cost breakdowns, spans/traces, logs, sampling
- Security: SSO, SAML, KMS integration, audit logs and data retention
- Benchmark plan and next steps for pilot

Transcript: 
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining on time, this is Maya from Redwood, with Diego and Samir on the call, uh before we start any quick intros?
[00:18] Aisha Rahman: hi i'm Aisha ran, runs infra and platform at ForgeWorks, benji is on the line too, we, we are exploring a new inference layer for our product search and doc-assist features.
[00:31] Benji Ortiz: yeah hi all, platform lead. main constraints are multitenant quotas, per-route rate limits and keeping costs predictable as usage spikes.
[00:45] Diego Alvarez: got it, thanks. quick question on current stack — we saw notes that you're on LangChain and use LlamaIndex for retrieval? how's that wired today?
[00:57] Tommy Park: yeah we're heavy on LangChain, LlamaIndex sits in front of our vector DB, we run a gateway service that fans out to different model backends, some internal self-host and some third-party. The gateway does routing, caching and rudimentary rate limiting.
[01:15] Samir Patel: when you say gateway is that a sidecar to each service or centralized?
[01:20] Tommy Park: centralized right now, it's an edge router written in go, we do prefix caching on some queries, KV cache is in-memory but not shared across nodes which sucks.
[01:32] Claire Ng: and we have residency constraints for EU customers, so any private deployment has to sit in our EU region.
[01:40] Maya Chen: perfect — that aligns with options we typically outline. quick overview: Redwood has three ops modes — hosted API for fastest path, Dedicated for reserved capacity (predictable throughput), and Private which we can run in your VPC or on-prem with a customer-managed control plane. Each has tradeoffs for latency, cost and network control.
[01:58] Benji Ortiz: can you describe the gateway placement options? we want to avoid rewriting our whole gateway service.
[02:08] Diego Alvarez: absolutely. Two common patterns: 1) Edge gateway (your current centralized router) forwards requests to Redwood's hosted endpoint — minimal code change, SDK calls or HTTP proxy. 2) Deploy Redwood sidecar agent or onboard via our SDK inside the service — this gives you tighter batching and local caching options. Sidecar also allows continuous batching and better KV cache locality. Both patterns support LangChain/LlamaIndex through adapters or direct SDK calls.
[02:35] Aisha Rahman: is the SDK python-first? we have a mix python/go services.
[02:41] Maya Chen: Python, Node, and Go clients are official. We also have thin http adapter if you want to call from any runtime. For LangChain specifically we have a connector we've validated with common chains; for LlamaIndex there's a community adapter and a Redwood-maintained integration guide.
[03:00] Tommy Park: you mentioned continuous batching — does sidecar automatically batch across requests? how does that affect latency spikes and tail p99?
[03:10] Diego Alvarez: good question. Sidecar does adaptive batching — it groups requests within short windows primarily by model and sequence profile. For p50 you often see improved throughput and cost. For p99 we keep a per-request latency SLO by using fast-path routing and can break large requests out to avoid head-of-line blocking. There's also prefix/KV caching which reduces tokens sent.
[03:33] Benji Ortiz: about quotas — we want tenant-level quotas and per-route limits and also want to surface usage to our billing system. Can Redwood enforce per-tenant rate limits?
[03:45] Samir Patel: yes — we support tenant-level quotas and per-route throttles. In hosted mode you can use our API keys scoped per-tenant. In Dedicated or Private you can map tenant IDs to tokens and enforce via our policy layer. We also expose webhook and telemetry streams for token-usage and cost so you can sync to your billing. There is some config around burst capacity — you can set allowed bursts and then define fallbacks.
[04:10] Claire Ng: what's fallback behavior if we exceed capacity — would requests queue or fail? and how is backpressure signaled to the gateway?
[04:18] Diego Alvarez: by default we rate limit with a 429 and provide retry-after headers. In Dedicated you can configure burst capacity and overflow routing to cheaper model variants. There's also an optional local-circuit behavior in sidecar where low-priority requests can be queued for a short window before failing. For important traffic you can set up a canary/buffering path.
[04:38] Aisha Rahman: security — we need SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs and KMS integration for key management. Any show-stoppers?
[04:47] Maya Chen: we support SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC in the console, and audit logs are exportable. For KMS we integrate with AWS KMS and a few enterprise HSM providers for Private deployments. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption and customer-managed keys via KMS for encryption at rest.
[05:08] Benji Ortiz: EU data residency — hosted can be in EU but we may prefer Private so we're fully isolated. What does Private look like operationally?
[05:18] Samir Patel: Private is essentially our runtime installed inside your VPC with a lightweight control plane contact. For fully air-gapped we can run without remote control plane; there are operational tradeoffs for updates/patches. In Private you get direct network control, your own telemetry streams, and we can integrate with your KMS and SIEM for logs.
[05:36] Tommy Park: can we run it on our existing k8s clusters?
[05:39] Diego Alvarez: yes — Private supports k8s helm charts and a container-based bundle. We also support an appliance for on-prem bare-metal. We document kernel/driver requirements for GPU acceleration if you want dedicated inference with GPUs.
[05:55] Aisha Rahman: let's get into SDK compatibility — we use LangChain abstractions and LlamaIndex retrieval. Any code changes needed?
[06:05] Maya Chen: you can either swap the model call in your chain to the Redwood SDK client (few lines) or keep your gateway and proxy to Redwood as an HTTP endpoint. For LlamaIndex we provide a connector that implements the retriever interface — mostly configuration and small adapter shim. We've seen customers do a phased approach: proxy-first to validate correctness then sidecar for performance.
[06:28] Tommy Park: if we proxy-first we lose batching and local cache advantages; is there an easy migration path?
[06:34] Samir Patel: absolute. We usually recommend proxy-first: change target endpoint, run functional tests. Once validated we deploy sidecar to hot paths and use feature flags to route a percentage of traffic to sidecar for benchmarking.
[06:50] Benji Ortiz: observability — what hooks do you expose? we need traces tied to our span IDs and token-level breakdowns.
[06:58] Diego Alvarez: we emit structured logs, traces (OpenTelemetry compatible), and detailed token-level metrics. Traces can propagate your span IDs if you pass the trace header. Token-level cost per-request, per-model, and per-route metrics are in the telemetry API and in the Console dashboards. You can set sampling rates for traces to control volume.
[07:18] Claire Ng: token-level metrics are great — how big is the telemetry payload? do we stream it or poll?
[07:24] Samir Patel: both: we have webhook streaming for events and a metrics ingestion endpoint (push). For high-volume customers we recommend streaming to your SIEM or a collector to avoid polling.
[07:34] Aisha Rahman: regarding latency — our p95 for search augmentation needs to be < 250ms. How realistic on hosted vs dedicated?
[07:44] Diego Alvarez: hosted in EU region usually hits 120-200ms for small prompt sizes on our faster model profiles. Dedicated (pinned GPU pools) offers more consistent p95 — we offer SLA-backed latency tiers. Private can be lowest-latency if you colocate near your services and use GPU instances. We'll include perf numbers in the TCO sheet.
[08:03] Tommy Park: any support for streaming responses? we use streaming to render partial answers in UI.
[08:09] Maya Chen: yes, streaming with SSE and websockets is supported across all modes; function-calling semantics are supported too.
[08:16] Benji Ortiz: about quotas — do you support different quota buckets per environment (staging vs prod)?
[08:22] Samir Patel: yes, separate API keys/environments and quotas are standard. You can also have per-tenant throttle policies.
[08:30] Aisha Rahman: licensing and cost discussion — high level?
[08:34] Maya Chen: hosted is usage-based; Dedicated is reserved capacity with month-to-month commits or annual for discounts; Private has a platform license + support contract. We'll share a TCO spreadsheet factoring per-token cost, reserved capacity amortization, and network egress.
[08:52] Benji Ortiz: can we do a pilot on hosted with traffic mirrored from our gateway?
[08:57] Diego Alvarez: yes mirror + proxy is common. You can mirror requests to Redwood for evaluation without impacting production. We'll set up a metrics pipeline to compare latency and token usage.
[09:10] Claire Ng: one more security Q: how do you handle PII redaction and retention?
[09:16] Samir Patel: we support configurable retention windows and automatic redaction hooks. For Hosted you can opt-in to not retain request/response logs; for Private you control retention entirely. We can also sign a data processing addendum for EU data protection.
[09:30] Tommy Park: let's talk about the benchmark — what would you need from us?
[09:34] Diego Alvarez: a sample prompt set, representative traffic profile (QPS distribution, size distributions), a few example long-form sequences, and if possible a small dataset for retrieving via LlamaIndex to exercise retrieval+generation. If you want a hosted trial we'll run an initial smoke test, then a Dedicated/Private throughput run on the side.
[09:55] Aisha Rahman: timeline — we need to decide by end of month so we'd like a pilot this week. is that feasible?
[10:02] Maya Chen: yes we can do a lightweight hosted pilot in 3-5 days. Dedicated pilot needs a little more prep, but we can run a benchmark within a week. Private will take longer due to VPC setup.
[10:14] Benji Ortiz: network diagram — we have strict egress controls. If we do Private, will Redwood need any inbound connections?
[10:22] Samir Patel: for Private with customer-managed control plane you can configure it to not allow inbound from outside your VPC. There's an option for a minimal control-plane tunnel for management, but we can operate fully air-gapped with manual updates. We'll need your network diagram to surface required endpoints and ports.
[10:38] Claire Ng: any gotchas with our current LlamaIndex usage? we use custom retrievers and chunking logic.
[10:44] Diego Alvarez: most custom retrievers map to our adapter layer. Chunking affects token counts — we can work with Tommy on token accounting and show you per-chunk cost impacts. Also consider local pre-filtering before hitting the model to reduce unnecessary tokens.
[10:59] Tommy Park: do you support quantized model variants we can route to for cheaper runs?
[11:04] Maya Chen: yes, we offer model variants with quantization profiles; in Dedicated you can pin quantized runners for cost savings. We also support automated routing to cheaper variants when quality thresholds are met.
[11:18] Aisha Rahman: can Redwood integrate with our feature flagging so we can ramp traffic?
[11:23] Samir Patel: yes, many customers use LaunchDarkly or internal flags to roll out sidecar traffic percentages. We can also do A/B rollouts via routing policies in the Console.
[11:35] Benji Ortiz: about observability again — will we see per-request prompt/response payloads in logs?
[11:41] Diego Alvarez: logs can include payloads but data controls let you disable it; token-level aggregates are always available. For privacy you'd likely disable payload retention and keep derived metrics.
[11:55] Claire Ng: what's the expected integration effort for sidecar rollout? team size and time?
[12:01] Maya Chen: small teams can do a sidecar pilot in 1-2 sprints. Typically 1 SE + 1 infra eng to set up, 1 dev to wire SDK or proxy config. We'll help with a portability checklist and runbook.
[12:15] Tommy Park: any pitfalls with k8s Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and batching behavior?
[12:20] Diego Alvarez: autoscaling can interact with batching — if you scale pods too aggressively you lose batching efficiency. We recommend sizing and burst policies that balance latency vs throughput. Our sidecar can expose metrics to inform HPA and you can set target CPU/memory based on observed throughput.
[12:39] Aisha Rahman: are there customers using Redwood behind an internal gateway pattern for multi-cloud?
[12:45] Samir Patel: yes, multiple customers run a central gateway that routes to Redwood in multiple regions or to different Dedicated clusters. We have smart routing policies for latency/cost.
[12:58] Benji Ortiz: for the pilot, can we mirror traffic and also run a dedicated benchmark to see cost per 1M requests estimate?
[13:05] Diego Alvarez: yes mirror plus dedicated benchmark. We'll need sample traffic and a target SLA to size reserved capacity for Dedicated.
[13:18] Tommy Park: topline question — if we start hosted and hit cost constraints, how hard is migration to Dedicated?
[13:26] Maya Chen: we've migrated multiple customers; typically it's a config/route change and model pinning. For stateful caches you may want to migrate caches; we provide migration playbooks. It's not trivial but it's planned as a live migration path.
[13:42] Aisha Rahman: can you share a handoff doc for our infra folks that lists ports, headers, and required ops work?
[13:48] Maya Chen: yes we'll share an integration checklist and a sample network diagram.
[13:52] Benji Ortiz: competitive question — are there features where Redwood differs materially from Anthropic/Vertex?
[13:58] Samir Patel: Redwood focuses on inference economics: unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, first-class batching/cache, and observability tied to token economics. Others may provide access but less focus on production controls and rollouts.
[14:15] Tommy Park: noise in transcription
[14:18] Claire Ng: haha i heard that too

-- Middle of call, deeper technical dive and occasional crosstalk (transcription imperfect) --

[22:05] Diego Alvarez: for the benchmark i'll set up a harness that can replay your traffic shape at variable qps and sequence lengths. We'll run both hosted small-model profile and a Dedicated GPU-backed run to compare latency and tokens per response.
[22:22] Tommy Park: please include our retrieval path — we want to exercise retrieval+generation combined.
[22:30] Samir Patel: noted. For retrieval we can deploy a local LlamaIndex adapter that queries your vector DB; we'll include that in the harness.
[22:40] Aisha Rahman: retention/PII again — will the harness send real data? we prefer sanitized data.
[22:46] Diego Alvarez: yes use sanitized dataset, or we can obfuscate at rest.

[30:05] Benji Ortiz: a quick question on rate limiting headers — do you provide granular headers for remaining quota?
[30:12] Diego Alvarez: yes we include remaining quota, limit, reset time and a cost-estimate header optionally.
[30:20] Claire Ng: will that tie into our billing system easily?
[30:23] Samir Patel: we can export per-tenant usage daily; for near real-time you can subscribe to webhooks.

[36:16] Maya Chen: recap: 1) ForgeWorks to share sample prompts, traffic profile, and network diagram by 7 Apr. 2) Redwood SE to run hosted smoke test and Dedicated throughput benchmark; deliver initial report by 9 Apr. 3) Redwood AE to share pricing and TCO sheet by 8 Apr. 4) Schedule Private deployment follow-up demo week of 13 Apr.
[36:40] Benji Ortiz: that sounds right. also please include our compliance contact for SOC2 doc review.
[36:46] Maya Chen: will do. Diego anything to add on technical notes?
[36:50] Diego Alvarez: just that we'll include a short runbook for sidecar rollout and notes on HPA/batching tradeoffs.
[36:58] Samir Patel: and we'll surface expected telemetry payloads and retention defaults so your SREs can plan pipeline capacity.

[41:10] Aisha Rahman: any final blockers from your side?
[41:14] Maya Chen: none — sounds like alignment.
[41:18] Tommy Park: i'll get the sample prompt set over after the call.
[41:22] Claire Ng: i'll share the network diagram and compliance contact.
[41:26] Benji Ortiz: thanks all.

[41:30] Maya Chen: great, thanks everyone we'll follow up with the items.

[41:36] Samir Patel: thanks all, bye.
